nameStory: Perfoliate honeysuckle gets its name from its most distinctive feature - the way its uppermost leaves appear to be pierced right through by the stem! The word 'perfoliate' comes from Latin meaning 'through the leaf,' describing how the stem seems to magically grow through the center of these special leaves. It's also called Italian woodbine since it's native to parts of Europe including Italy.
description: Perfoliate honeysuckle is a vigorous climbing vine that can scramble up to 26 feet high, wrapping itself around trees, fences, and anything else it can grab onto. This deciduous climber produces masses of incredibly fragrant, cream-colored flowers tinged with pink that bloom in midsummer. What makes this honeysuckle instantly recognizable is its unique uppermost leaves that look like the stem is growing right through them, creating a distinctive cup-like appearance. Though native to Europe, it has naturalized in some parts of northeastern North America.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: The uppermost leaves are fused together around the stem, creating a cup or disc shape that the stem appears to pierce through - this perfoliate feature is unmistakable and unique among honeysuckles

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Masses of tubular, cream-colored flowers with a pink blush emerge from the center of the fused upper leaves, releasing an intensely sweet, almost intoxicating fragrance especially in the evening

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: A vigorous twining vine that climbs by wrapping its stems around supports, reaching impressive heights and forming dense tangles in favorable conditions

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lower leaves are opposite, oval-shaped, and smooth-edged with a bluish-green color, but it's the dramatically different upper leaves that steal the show

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small orange to red berries cluster at the center of the perfoliate leaves in late summer, sitting like jewels in their leafy cups

habitat: In New England, perfoliate honeysuckle is quite rare with only a few documented sightings, typically found in disturbed areas, old gardens, or forest edges where it has escaped cultivation. It prefers partial shade to full sun and adapts to various soil types, often climbing over shrubs and into the canopy of small trees. Look for it near old homesites or in areas where European plants were historically cultivated.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge in late spring, with the distinctive perfoliate upper leaves becoming apparent as the vine begins its vigorous growth phase.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification time when the intensely fragrant cream and pink flowers bloom from the center of the fused leaves, creating a spectacular and unmistakable display.
seasonality.fall: Orange to red berries ripen in the leafy cups, and leaves may turn yellow before dropping, revealing the vine's twining woody stems.
seasonality.winter: Bare twining stems remain wrapped around supports, with the woody vine structure visible - look for opposite branching pattern and smooth bark on younger stems.

funFact: The perfoliate leaves aren't actually pierced by the stem - they're two opposite leaves that have completely fused together at their bases, creating what botanists call a 'connate-perfoliate' arrangement that's so perfect it looks like nature's magic trick!
confusionNotes: The perfoliate leaves make this honeysuckle nearly impossible to confuse with any other plant once you know what to look for. Other honeysuckles have separate leaves, never fused ones, so if you see stem-pierced leaves on a climbing honeysuckle, you've found the rare perfoliate species!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Italian honeysuckle,' this species is actually native to much of Europe, not just Italy. With only two recorded observations in New England, finding this plant would be quite a botanical treasure - many of our common honeysuckles are also non-native, but this one remains genuinely rare in our region.
compareHints: While New England has many honeysuckle species, perfoliate honeysuckle is the only one with fused upper leaves that the stem appears to grow through. Japanese honeysuckle has separate, oval leaves and stays green later into fall, while native coral honeysuckle has separate, more rounded leaves and bright red flowers. The perfoliate feature immediately distinguishes this species from all other honeysuckles in our region.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the invasive Japanese, Morrow's, and Tatarian honeysuckles that dominate many New England areas, American fly-honeysuckle has distinctively paired berries and a much more restrained growth habit.
Japanese honeysuckle is unique among New England honeysuckles for its white-to-yellow color change and semi-evergreen leaves.
Unlike native fly honeysuckles which have flowers in clusters and blue or black berries, Morrow's honeysuckle has flowers and berries strictly in pairs with red fruit.
Unlike native American fly-honeysuckle which stays small and has paired flowers on long stalks, Amur honeysuckle grows into a large shrub with flowers sitting directly on the branches.
Among New England honeysuckles, coral honeysuckle is the only one with scentless, coral-red tubular flowers and that distinctive leaf-fusion around the stem.
Among New England's honeysuckles, glaucous honeysuckle is the only climbing species with that distinctive waxy blue-green leaf coating and cup-forming fused upper leaves.
Unlike our native fly honeysuckles which have flowers in clusters and blue or black berries, Tatarian honeysuckle always has paired flowers and red berries.
Mountain fly-honeysuckle differs from American fly honeysuckle by having much fuzzier leaves and preferring higher elevation habitats.
Among New England's honeysuckles, the dense coating of soft hairs immediately separates this species from smooth-leaved Japanese honeysuckle or the only slightly hairy American fly honeysuckle.
Fly honeysuckle stands out from other honeysuckles in New England by its paired red berries and shrubby growth habit - most others either climb like vines or have different colored berries.
Unlike the vigorous vining Japanese honeysuckle, winter honeysuckle is a well-behaved shrub that doesn't climb.
Unlike the more common American fly honeysuckle which prefers drier woods, swamp fly honeysuckle demands wet feet and boggy conditions.

Unlike the ubiquitous Japanese honeysuckle which blooms white to yellow and has simple opposite leaves, common honeysuckle has those distinctive fused upper leaves and more intensely fragrant flowers.
Unlike the invasive Asian honeysuckles that plague New England (Japanese, Morrow's, Amur), twinberry honeysuckle doesn't spread aggressively and has the unique twin-berry-in-red-bracts feature.
Unlike the aggressive Japanese honeysuckle that stays white then turns yellow, grape honeysuckle flowers age to pink.
Unlike its weedy relatives like Japanese honeysuckle (which climbs) or Morrow's honeysuckle (which has red berries), sweetberry honeysuckle stays compact and produces edible blue fruit.
